title: Duplicate Zeros
statement: `arr` is an integer array whose length cannot change. Rewrite it in place so that every `0` is followed by an extra `0`, with the elements after it moved one position to the right to make room. Values pushed beyond the last index are lost. The function returns nothing; the result is the contents of `arr` after it finishes.
notes:
## Intuition

Inserting a zero and shifting the tail right every time works, but costs O(n²). Look instead at where each element ends up: it moves right by the number of zeros in front of it. Picture a longer array of length `n + zeros` that has room for every extra zero; each element's final slot in it is known. Filling from the right end with two pointers moving in the same direction, a slow `read` and a `write` that stays ahead of it, never overwrites a value that still has to be read.

## Approach

1. Count the zeros of `arr` into `zeros`.
2. Put `read` on the last real index and `write` on the last index of the imagined array, `n + zeros - 1`.
3. While `read < write`, copy `arr[read]` to `arr[write]` if `write` is inside the real array, then move `write` left.
4. If `arr[read]` is a zero, write a second zero at the new `write` (again only if it is inside) and move `write` left once more.
5. Move `read` left. When the pointers meet, no zero lies in front of them, so that prefix is already in place.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [1,0,2,3,0,4,5,0]`, `n = 8`, `zeros = 3`, so `read = 7`, `write = 10`.

- `read = 7` (a 0): slots 10 and 9 are past the end; `write` becomes 8.
- `read = 6` (5): slot 8 is past the end; `write` becomes 7.
- `read = 5` (4): `arr[7] = 4`; `write` becomes 6.
- `read = 4` (a 0): `arr[6] = 0` and `arr[5] = 0`; `write` becomes 4.
- `read = 3` and `read = 2`: `arr[4] = 3`, `arr[3] = 2`; `write` becomes 2.
- `read = 1` (a 0): `arr[2] = 0` and `arr[1] = 0`; `write` becomes 0, equal to `read`, so the loop stops.

The array is now `[1,0,0,2,3,0,0,4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass to count and at most one backward pass.
- Space: O(1): two indices and a counter.

## Pitfalls

- Copying left to right overwrites elements before they are read; go from the right.
- Guard every write with `write < n`. A zero near the end may keep one copy and lose the other, as in `[1,2,3,0]`.
- Stop when `read` meets `write`; the rest needs no moves, and continuing would corrupt it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | the fixed length of `arr` |
| `zeros` | how many zeros `arr` holds |
| `value` | each element while counting |
| `read` | index of the original element being placed |
| `write` | its target slot in the imagined longer array |

narration.2: Remember the fixed length; anything written at or past it is thrown away.
narration.4: Scan every element once to count the zeros.
narration.5: Each zero will push everything after it one place to the right.
narration.7: read starts on the last original element.
narration.8: write starts on the last slot of an imagined array long enough for every extra zero.
narration.9: Keep going while some zero still lies at or before read; once the pointers meet, the rest is already in place.
narration.10: Only write when the target slot exists in the real array.
narration.11: Copy the element to its final position.
narration.13: That slot is used up, whether or not it was real, so move write one place left.
narration.14: A zero needs a second copy just before the first one.
narration.18: The extra copy used a slot, so move write left again.
narration.20: Move on to the previous original element.
